title: Hip Replacement Recovery Week by Week
meta_description: Follow a UK hip replacement recovery timeline covering walking, exercises, driving, work, warning signs and when to contact your surgical team.
excerpt: Follow a UK hip replacement recovery timeline covering walking, exercises, driving, work, warning signs and when to contact your surgical team.
direct_answer: Recovery after hip replacement is gradual and varies by person. NICE recommends rehabilitation within 24 hours of surgery, followed by a clear home exercise plan. The NHS advises daily walking as comfortable, prescribed exercises, no driving for at least six weeks, and a return to work often around six weeks depending on the job and recovery.
author: Louis Maxwell
content:
What are the key points about hip replacement recovery?

  • NICE recommends rehabilitation on the day of surgery where possible, and no later than 24 hours afterwards.
  • Follow your hospital's exercise and movement plan; recovery milestones vary with health, surgical approach and the demands of daily life.
  • The NHS advises waiting at least six weeks before driving and checking that your doctor considers you fit to drive.
  • Get urgent help for chest pain, sudden breathlessness, a hot or leaking wound, fever, or sudden painful calf swelling.

What happens during the first 24 hours after hip replacement?

NICE recommends physiotherapy or occupational therapy on the day of surgery where possible, and within 24 hours at the latest. Early rehabilitation should cover safe mobilisation, everyday activities and a home exercise programme. Your surgical team decides when it is safe for you to stand and walk.

What is a realistic hip replacement recovery timeline?

Recovery is not identical for everyone. Use this table as a planning guide, then follow the milestones set by your surgical and rehabilitation team.

StageTypical focusSafe milestonesWhen to ask for help
Day 0 to dischargePain control, circulation exercises and supported mobilisationTransfers, short walks and stairs if required for homeYou cannot manage the discharge plan or symptoms are worsening
Weeks 1–2Prescribed exercises, wound care and short regular walksIncreasing household movement with the advised walking aidThe wound becomes hotter, redder, opens or leaks; fever develops
Weeks 3–6Build walking and everyday activity graduallyReduce aids only when advised and when walking is safe and controlledPain or function is deteriorating rather than gradually improving
Weeks 6–12Strength, balance, work and driving decisionsDriving only when medically fit and able to control the car safelySelf-directed rehabilitation is not meeting agreed goals
After 12 weeksProgress towards longer-term activity goalsLow-impact activity progressed with individual clinical advicePersistent limitation, instability or increasing pain

How much should I walk after a hip replacement?

The NHS advises walking every day as far as is comfortable and completing the exercises prescribed by your physiotherapist. Increase distance gradually rather than making large jumps. Use the walking aid supplied by your team until they advise that your strength, balance and walking pattern are safe without it.

Which exercises should I do after hip replacement?

Do the exercises provided by your hospital physiotherapist because precautions and progression can differ. NICE says discharge advice should include clear rehabilitation goals, prescribed exercises and a contact for support. Supervised rehabilitation should be offered when self-directed rehabilitation is not meeting goals or daily activities remain difficult.

When can I drive after a hip replacement?

The NHS advises waiting at least six weeks and checking with your doctor that you are fit to drive. You must be able to enter and leave the car, control it safely and perform an emergency stop without hesitation. Check your motor insurance requirements before driving.

When can I return to work after hip replacement?

The NHS says returning to work often takes about six weeks, but timing depends on recovery and the type of work. Desk work, commuting, prolonged sitting, lifting and manual duties create different demands. Agree a phased return with your surgical team, employer or occupational health service where appropriate.

What should I avoid while the hip is recovering?

Follow the precautions given by your surgical team. The NHS advises avoiding crossed legs, low seating, heavy lifting, jumping, sudden turns and activities with a high risk of falling during recovery. Do not substitute general internet advice for approach-specific instructions from your own hospital.

Which warning signs need urgent medical help?

Seek urgent clinical advice if the wound becomes increasingly red, hot, swollen, painful or starts leaking, or if you develop fever. Call 999 for chest pain or sudden severe breathlessness. Sudden calf pain and one-sided swelling can indicate a blood clot and need urgent assessment.

Frequently asked questions

How long does hip replacement recovery take?

Many everyday activities improve over the first 6 to 12 weeks, but strength and confidence can continue improving for several months. Your health, surgical approach, home circumstances and rehabilitation needs affect the timeline.

How long will I need crutches after hip replacement?

There is no fixed deadline. Use the frame, sticks or crutches supplied by your team until you can walk safely with an acceptable pattern and your physiotherapist advises progression.

Can I sleep on my side after hip replacement?

Follow your hospital's advice because wound position, surgical approach and individual precautions differ. Use the recommended pillows or positioning and ask your team before changing sleeping position.

Is swelling normal after hip replacement?

Some swelling can occur during recovery and may increase after activity. Contact your team if swelling is sudden, worsening, associated with calf pain, or accompanied by wound changes, fever, chest pain or breathlessness.

When can I drive after hip replacement?

The NHS advises waiting at least six weeks and confirming that your doctor considers you fit. You must be able to control the vehicle and perform an emergency stop safely, and you should check your insurance.

What if home rehabilitation is not working?

Contact the rehabilitation team named in your discharge plan. NICE recommends supervised group or individual outpatient rehabilitation when self-directed rehabilitation is not meeting goals or daily activities remain difficult.

Which sources support this recovery guide?

  1. NICE guideline NG157: Joint replacement (primary): hip, knee and shoulder (2020), postoperative rehabilitation recommendations.
  2. NHS: Recovering from a hip replacement, reviewed UK recovery, driving, work and activity guidance.
  3. NHS: Preparing for a hip replacement, preparation and home-planning guidance.

Educational information for people in the United Kingdom, not a personal recovery plan. Follow the instructions from your surgical and rehabilitation team. Clinically reviewed by Louis Maxwell, First Contact Physiotherapist, HCPC PH128483. Last reviewed 23 October 2026.
